lead: A laminate is several fibre-reinforced plies bonded with chosen fibre angles. Each ply is orthotropic, so its stiffness in laminate axes must be rotated first. Summing the rotated plies through the thickness gives three matrices: A for extension, B for extension–bending coupling, and D for bending. These matrices turn mid-plane strains and curvatures into loads and moments per unit width. Engineers use them for wing skins, helicopter blades, pressure vessels and composite beams, where the stacking sequence is chosen to place stiffness where it is needed.
prereq: You need ply stiffness and rotated Qbar from 6.7, and plate bending from 6.1.

sections.h3: From plies to A, B, D

blocks.text: A laminate is a stack of fibre-reinforced plies bonded together. Each ply has its own fibre angle. The stacking sequence lists those angles through the thickness, for example [0/90]s. The subscript s means the stack is symmetric about the mid-plane.
Measure the through-thickness coordinate z from the mid-plane. The mid-plane is z=0. Ply k occupies z<sub>k−1</sub> to z<sub>k</sub>. Its thickness is t<sub>k</sub>=z<sub>k</sub>−z<sub>k−1</sub>.

In laminate axes x and y, ply k has reduced stiffness Qbarij, where i,j=1,2,6. Qbar comes from rotating the ply stiffness by its fibre angle; the rotation is in 6.7. Qbar means stiffness in laminate axes.

blocks.where: A<sub>ij</sub> is extensional stiffness per unit width (N/mm); Qbar is in N/mm²; z is in mm; the sum is over all plies k.
B<sub>ij</sub> is extension–bending coupling stiffness (N); the factor ½ comes from integrating z through the thickness.
D<sub>ij</sub> is bending stiffness per unit width (N·mm); the factor ⅓ comes from integrating z² through the thickness.

blocks.text: The in-plane strain in a ply varies linearly with z. Integrating that strain through the thickness produces A, B and D. A weights each ply by its thickness. D uses the difference (z<sub>k</sub>³ − z<sub>k−1</sub>³); for a thin ply this difference is roughly z<sup>2</sup> times the ply thickness, so plies far from the mid-plane dominate bending stiffness.
The three matrices form the laminate constitutive law. N and M are in-plane force and moment per unit width. ε⁰ is mid-plane strain. κ is curvature.

blocks.where: N is in-plane force per unit width (N/mm); M is moment per unit width (N); ε⁰ is mid-plane strain; κ is curvature (1/mm).

blocks.text: For a symmetric laminate, B=0. Extension and bending uncouple: N=Aε⁰ and M=Dκ. For an unsymmetric laminate, B is not zero. An axial load then causes curvature, and a moment causes extension.

A11 is the extensional stiffness along x. D11 is the bending stiffness for curvature κ<sub>x</sub>. Stacking sequence changes D much more than A. A balanced laminate has equal +θ and −θ plies, which removes some shear–extension coupling. A symmetric stacking sequence removes B about the mid-plane.
For a laminate strip bending along the 1 direction, let M<sub>1</sub> be moment per unit width and κ<sub>1</sub> curvature. For a symmetric laminate, M<sub>1</sub>=D11κ<sub>1</sub>+D12κ<sub>2</sub>.

blocks.where: EI is strip bending stiffness for κ<sub>2</sub>=0 (N·mm²); b is width (mm); D11 is laminate bending stiffness per unit width (N·mm).

blocks.text: The formula EI=bD11 applies when κ2=0, as in cylindrical plate bending, or when D12=0. It is not the general narrow-beam result.

blocks.where: EI is narrow-beam bending stiffness for a symmetric laminate (N·mm²); D12 and D22 are the other bending stiffness terms per unit width (N·mm).

blocks.text: For a narrow beam free to anticlastic curvature, M2=0. Then κ2=−(D12/D22)κ1, and the effective stiffness is the second formula. A wide beam behaves more like a plate, and one beam stiffness may not describe it.
The D terms have units of moment per unit width per curvature. Multiplying by width b gives N·mm², the same unit as EI in ordinary beam theory.

figure.caption: A symmetric cross-ply laminate; the mid-plane is the reference z=0.

spec.aria: Stack of four plies in a symmetric 0/90/90/0 laminate with thickness coordinates.

examples.question: A [0/90]s laminate has four plies, each 0.125 mm thick. For a 0° ply Q11=140.9 GPa and Q22=10.1 GPa. For a 90° ply the roles swap, so Qbar11=10.1 GPa. Find A11 per unit width, D11 per unit width, and bD11 for a 100 mm wide strip restrained so κ2=0. State B11. Say what extra terms a narrow beam free to curl sideways needs.
steps: Total thickness is 4×0.125=0.5 mm. With z=0 at the mid-plane, the interfaces are z0=−0.25, z1=−0.125, z2=0, z3=0.125, z4=0.25 mm.
Ply 1 is 0° from −0.25 to −0.125 mm. Ply 2 is 90° from −0.125 to 0 mm. Ply 3 is 90° from 0 to 0.125 mm. Ply 4 is 0° from 0.125 to 0.25 mm.

For D11, use each interval separately. For each 0° interval, Q11(z<sub>k</sub>³−z<sub>k−1</sub>³)=140.9×0.013671875=1.926367 GPa·mm³. For each 90° interval, Q22(z<sub>k</sub>³−z<sub>k−1</sub>³)=10.1×0.001953125=0.019727 GPa·mm³.

bD11=100×1297.4=129,739.6 N·mm²=1.2974×10⁵ N·mm². This equals EI only when κ2=0 or D12=0. For a narrow beam free to anticlastic curvature, M2=0 and EI=b(D11−D12²/D22). D12 and D22 are not given here, so the narrow-beam EI cannot be completed from these data; bD11 is its upper bound.
B11=0 because the laminate is symmetric about the mid-plane.
examples.answer: A11=37.75 GPa·mm=37,750 N/mm; D11=1,297.4 N·mm; bD11=129,739.6 N·mm² (1.2974×10⁵ N·mm²) for κ2=0; B11=0. A narrow beam free to curl sideways needs D12 and D22: EI=b(D11−D12²/D22).

traps: Using Q instead of Qbar for a 90° ply. At 90°, Qbar11 equals Q22, not Q11.
Measuring z from the bottom surface. All z values must be from the mid-plane, positive upward.
Expecting B=0 for every laminate. Only a symmetric stacking sequence gives B=0 about the mid-plane.
Forgetting the unit change from GPa·mm to N/mm. 1 GPa·mm = 1000 N/mm.
Using EI=bD11 for a narrow beam that is free to curl sideways. That formula needs κ2=0 or D12=0; for a narrow symmetric beam use EI=b(D11−D12²/D22).

quiz.q: What are the matrices A, B and D called?
quiz.a: A is extensional stiffness, B is extension–bending coupling stiffness, and D is bending stiffness.

quiz.q: Why is B zero for a symmetric laminate?
quiz.a: Each ply above the mid-plane has a mirror ply below it at −z. Its contribution to B changes sign, so the sum cancels.

quiz.q: A [0/90]s laminate has four plies, each 0.2 mm thick. Q11=150 GPa and Q22=10 GPa. Find A11 per unit width.
A [90/0]s laminate is changed to [0/90]s with the same plies. What happens to D11 and why?
quiz.a: D11 increases. The 0° plies move to the outer surfaces, and D weights each ply by z³, so their contribution grows strongly.

quiz.q: A symmetric laminate has D11=2000 N·mm and is restrained so κ2=0. A strip of width 50 mm bends along the 1 direction. Find EI.
Why can an unsymmetric laminate warp after cure?
quiz.a: B is not zero. Cure shrinkage and thermal strain produce effective axial loads and moments that couple extension and bending, so the plate curves out of plane.

quiz.q: Why does D depend on z³ while A depends only on ply thickness?
quiz.a: Bending strain varies linearly with z, and the moment is the integral of stress times z. Integrating z² through the thickness gives the z³ difference in D.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial laminate design tools build A, B, D for many plies and pass them to finite element solvers. Optimisation searches stacking sequences for stiffness, strength, buckling and cost. Impact damage and delamination need models beyond classical laminate theory. Aeroelastic tailoring uses bend–twist coupling to reduce gust loads. Search for classical laminate theory, ABD matrix, and composite beam stiffness.
